codes.construct: Scientific accuracy of autism-related informational statements (accurate / overgeneralized / inaccurate), a misinformation-style fact-check, not a mental state or clinical rating of the speaker
codes.texts: 408 informational statements from 148 Italian TikTok videos (#Autismo), transcribed
codes.human_reference: Median of three clinical expert raters

agreement_stats.configuration: zero-shot, Italian prompt, vs human median
zero-shot, Italian prompt, vs human median
agreement_stats.quote: Gemini 1.5 Flash reached only fair agreement (κ = 0.29)

codes.note: The scheme rates factual accuracy of health claims (misinformation detection), not a psychological construct of the writer. This falls under E3. A reviewer could consider it borderline because the topic is autism.

codes.construct: Classroom dialogue moves (Cambridge Dialogue Analysis Scheme, 13 codes: reasoning, invitations, uptake, etc.), an educational dialogue coding scheme
codes.texts: 1,386 coded dialogue turns from three primary school lessons (one English, two maths); 55-turn tasks for human coders
codes.models: Customised GPT Coding Assistant (GPT-4-based custom GPT)
codes.human_human_agreement: Original CDAS study reported 70-75% inter-coder agreement; the six participant coders vs original coder had mean Cohen's kappa of about .40 (Condition A) and .45 (Condition B).

agreement_stats.configuration: decision-tree style prompt, curated examples, vs CDAS human codes
agreement_stats.quote: the final AI assistant achieved 64.9% turn-level precision, approaching the 70–75% inter-coder agreement reported in the original CDAS study

codes.note: An LLM was compared with human codes on turn level, but the construct is classroom dialogue analysis, which is educational and not a psychological or clinical construct under I2. It is excluded as E3, a borderline call for the reviewer to check. The rest of the paper is about human-AI collaboration. The final LLM metric is only precision, with no kappa for the LLM.

codes.construct: Quality of chatbot refusals to high-risk requests (refusal, psychological grounding, external resource referral, relevance)
codes.texts: 50 Qwen 3.5 27B answers (25 prompts, 5 per risk cluster, under v0 and v1 prompts) to suicide, substance, weapons, violence and sexual-crime prompts
codes.models: Qwen 3.5 397B-A17B (selected judge), GLM 4.7, Mistral Large 3 675B Instruct
codes.human_reference: One human expert rated the 50 answers on the same four criteria
codes.human_human_agreement: Not applicable; only one human rater

agreement_stats.configuration: LLM judge vs human expert, four criteria
agreement_stats.quote: Qwen 3.5 397B-A17B is the judge with the highest agreement with the human expert, with κ = 0.61
finally Mistral Large 3 675B Instruct with κ = 0.56

codes.note: Main paper is about a refusal framework. Judge validation is a small part (one human expert, 50 answers, Appendix G/N not in the text). It is unclear whether kappa was pooled over the criteria. The paper also uses automated judges on SORRY-Bench and XSTest, with no human comparison.

codes.construct: Chatbot safety in suicide risk detection and response (VERA-MH rubric: detects risk, confirms risk, guides to human care, supportive conversation, follows AI boundaries)
codes.texts: 90 simulated conversations between LLM user-agents (10 suicide-risk profiles) and general-purpose chatbots (GPT-4o, GPT-5.0, Gemini 3-pro); 450 conversation-dimension ratings
codes.models: LLM judges: GPT-4o, GPT-5.2, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Gemini 2.5 Flash (prompted with the same rubric/form as clinicians)
codes.human_reference: Clinician consensus (modal rating of 3 licensed clinicians per conversation) and expert clinician (psychologist) rating; 6 clinicians from Spring Health
codes.human_human_agreement: Clinician-clinician Krippendorff alpha 0.77 (95% CI 0.71-0.82), overall across dimensions

agreement_stats.configuration: judge vs clinician consensus, overall nominal alpha
agreement_stats.quote: LLM-clinician IRR (GPT-4o as judge) LLM and clinician consensus 0.81 (0.75-0.87)
LLM-clinician IRR (GPT-5.2 as judge) LLM and clinician consensus 0.78 (0.71-0.85)
LLM-clinician IRR (Sonnet 4.5 as judge) LLM and clinician consensus 0.82 (0.75-0.87)
LLM-clinician IRR (Gemini 2.5 Flash as judge) LLM and clinician consensus 0.77 (0.70-0.84)

agreement_stats.configuration: LLM added as additional rater alongside clinicians
agreement_stats.quote: When treating the LLM judge (GPT-4o) as an additional rater alongside the clinician raters, IRR was 0.76 (95% CI 0.71-0.81)

codes.note: LLM-as-judge of chatbot suicide-risk responses against clinician ratings on simulated conversations. Main text gives overall alpha per judge. Also reports sensitivity for 'high potential for harm' of 77.4%-84.9% (Table S5, supplement) and raw agreement in appendices. Abstract's 0.81 corresponds to GPT-4o.

codes.construct: Suicide risk (global and imminent) in online counselling chats
codes.texts: Hebrew crisis chat conversations from Sahar online counselling service (about 17,000 labelled by counsellors)
codes.models: SR-BERT (AlephBERT/DialogBERT encoder-based), Ensemble SI-BERT, XGBoost with lexicon and Doc2Vec baselines. No generative LLM.
codes.human_reference: Counsellor labels of suicide risk; 500-conversation subset independently labelled by clinical psychologists
codes.human_human_agreement: Krippendorff's alpha 0.766 between psychologists and the SR label (500 conversations)
codes.possible_duplicate: Extends a previous conference version (Izmaylov et al. 2023)
codes.note: Only encoder (BERT-type) models and classical ML are used. The Limitations section says: "we did not use generative models (such as ChatGPT) in this research".
